note: Which widgets owe the Validation Lab an independent check, and which do not. Hand written and reviewed, not derived: implementation.definition names src/core.ts#TYPES for 39 of 51 widgets, so the registry does not record where most widgets are implemented and the computing/presentational line cannot be read off it. The validator enforces that every widget appears exactly once, that a claimed check exists in parity.json, and that the awaiting count only falls. It does not enforce the judgement, which is the part a person has to make and defend in the reason.

expectations.parity: Computes a value an independent implementation could recompute. Owes a lab check; `check` names it once it exists.
expectations.none: Nothing to recompute: an input, a presentation, or a rule node whose conclusions are the reasoner's. `reason` says which.
expectations.blocked: Would owe a check, and cannot have a meaningful one yet. `reason` names the obstacle.

widgets.computes: Applies a declared ruleset: projects facts from a typed carrier, binds a parameter with its unit, evaluates N3, and extracts a classification against the ruleset's declared vocabulary.
widgets.reason: Checked by the Lab exhaustively rather than by sample: all three rulesets have finite input spaces, 46 cells in total, and check 23 reproduces every conclusion with a Python decision table and verifies the emitted receipt.
Draws what it is given and derives no value; its receipt is a presentation receipt.

widgets.computes: Point-in-polygon membership against the study area's outline, with the three relations kept apart -- inside, on the boundary, outside -- and the boundary case admitted or refused by a declared choice.
widgets.reason: Worth recomputing independently because the answer decides what the rest of a workflow sees, and because the edge cases are where implementations differ: a point exactly on a vertex, a point on a segment between two vertices, and a point inside an enclave that the outer ring contains. Shapely's `contains` and `touches` answer all three and can be compared directly against this widget's counts. The predicate itself is shared with the coverage check, so a disagreement here is a disagreement there.

widgets.computes: Computes the displacement between two point sets and the centre of each.

widgets.reason: Draws what it is given and derives no value.

widgets.computes: Cross-source record linkage: a blocking distance, a Jaro-Winkler or exact name comparison, binary contributions to a score, and three classes from two thresholds. The merge is what the classification licences.
widgets.reason: Worth recomputing independently because every part of it has a reference implementation to disagree with. Jaro-Winkler is a published algorithm with published values -- martha/marhta is 0.961 and dwayne/duane is 0.840 -- and the prefix adjustment has three parameters any of which can be got wrong silently. The clustering has its own rule, one record per source, which decides whether a third record joins a pair or is refused. And a lab notebook can answer the question this widget cannot: what the thresholds SHOULD be on real OSM and Overture data, which the release says are proposals rather than measurements.

widgets.computes: One value per group from two values of a key column, under a named operation. An independent implementation recomputes the derived row for each group of Snow's Table IX -- 40,046 houses minus 1,263 deaths is 38,783 houses without a death -- and recomputes which groups are skipped for want of an operand. The arithmetic is a subtraction and the check is cheap; what it is worth checking is the GROUPING, which is where a long table makes this easy to get wrong.
Displaces each point by a seeded random distance within an annulus.
Selects facilities within a radius of an area, which is a distance computation.

widgets.reason: Restates graded evidence as a register. It selects and presents; it derives no value.

It does compute -- a confidence threshold, a kind filter and a name requirement -- but its input comes from a live external source, so an independent recomputation cannot be pinned to a fixture without first freezing a response. The selection logic is unit-tested. Needs a frozen-response fixture before a lab check means anything.

widgets.computes: Totals of the rows agreeing on the key columns kept. An independent implementation -- a pandas groupby sum over the related Table VIII -- recomputes all six totals of the Snow contingency table and, separately, that a group holding an empty cell comes back as nothing known rather than as a smaller number. That second case is the one worth an independent check: pandas sums over a missing value by default, so the check is a comparison with the behaviour this widget deliberately does NOT have.
Dijkstra traversal, part-way edges and a corridor buffer, in one widget.

Which boundary part each table row names, under a declared normalisation, and the value each part carries as a result. An independent implementation recomputes the matched and unmatched counts and the value on every part: 32 of 32 sub-districts match on Snow's files after folding punctuation, 23 of 32 on the raw strings, and 33 parts carry a rate because Streatham is two polygons.

widgets.reason: Draws what it is given and derives no value.

widgets.reason: Expands to its members and asserts fw:claimsNoComputation. The members carry the checks.
Validates a supplied graph against its stated endpoints and lengths. The validation is unit-tested; nothing is recomputed from data.

widgets.computes: Generates a regular grid at a stated spacing in a projection.

widgets.reason: A supplied GeoTIFF, retained as given.

widgets.computes: Divides a numerator by a denominator and scales it, with a minimum denominator.

A key column brought from a second table onto these rows, matched on a shared column. An independent implementation -- a pandas left merge of Snow's Table VIII onto Table XII on `sub_district` -- recomputes which rows receive which category, how many are dropped for keys the second table does not carry, and that the row count is unchanged. The arithmetic is none; what is worth recomputing is the MATCHING, and in particular that an ambiguous key is refused rather than resolved to whichever row came first, which is the failure a merge implementation would silently commit.

widgets.note: Two checks cover this widget. 01-reproject recomputes the INVERSE transform, which the widget performed until release 0.1.0; 24-project-forward recomputes the FORWARD projection it performs from 0.2.0. The check named here is the one covering the current release, because this field answers whether what ships is checked. The validator reads one check per widget from parity.json and keeps the last entry, so a widget with two checks is recorded accurately in parity.json and narrowed to the live one here.

widgets.computes: Walking minutes from each distance at a stated speed, reading each row's declared unit.
widgets.reason: A division, so the arithmetic is not the interesting part. What a lab check would establish is that the unit is read rather than assumed -- a metre reading divided by metres-per-minute against a kilometre reading, which differ by a thousand. Owed.
